findings.description: The source asks a yes/no question: is there an absolute constant K such that, for every C > 0, all large n have at most K divisors in (n^{1/2}, n^{1/2}+Cn^{1/4})? The Lean statement `∀ C > 0, ∀ᶠ n in atTop, #{d ∈ Ioo ⌊√n⌋₊ ⌈√n + C n^(1/4)⌉₊ | d ∣ n} ≤ answer(sorry)` uses `answer(sorry)` as the witness K. It therefore presupposes a positive answer: if no such K exists, the statement is false for every value of the answer, and the negative answer cannot be recorded. The companion `parts.ii` (`∃ K, ...`, asserted as a theorem) presupposes 'yes' as well. The source records no conjectured direction. The integer interval `Ioo ⌊√n⌋₊ ⌈...⌉₊` itself correctly matches the real open interval.
findings.source_evidence: erdosproblems.com/887 (Wayback snapshot 2026): "Is there an absolute constant K such that, for every C>0, if n is sufficiently large then n has at most K divisors in (n^{1/2},n^{1/2}+Cn^{1/4})?" The status is OPEN and no expected answer is given. CONTRIBUTING prescribes `answer(sorry) ↔ P` for questions; the misformalization-labelled PR #68 converted such statements.
findings.suggested_fix: theorem erdos_887.parts.i : answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ K : ℕ, ∀ C > (0 : ℝ), ∀ᶠ n in atTop, #{ d ∈ Ioo ⌊√n⌋₊ ⌈√n + C * n^((1 : ℝ) / 4)⌉₊ | d ∣ n } ≤ K

findings.description: The theorem docstring says "conjecturally, there are no Lychrel numbers in base 10", and the module docstring calls this "one commonly stated conjectural direction". The cited source records the opposite conjecture: 196 and similar numbers are conjectured to BE Lychrel numbers. The Lean statement uses `answer(sorry)`, so the mathematics is intact, but the documented expected answer is inverted.
findings.source_evidence: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lychrel_number: "It is conjectured that 196 and other numbers that have not yet yielded a palindrome are Lychrel numbers, but no number in base ten has yet been proven to be Lychrel."
findings.suggested_fix: Reword the docstrings, e.g. "Are there no Lychrel numbers in base 10? It is conjectured that 196 is a Lychrel number, so the expected answer is no."

findings.description: The Lean statement restricts A to `Finset ℕ`. The problem comes from Erdős–Newman's question on bases for sets of integers, where the basis B ⊂ ℤ may contain negative integers, so a square can also be written as b + b' with b < 0 < b'. A positive answer over ℤ implies one over ℕ, but not conversely, and no equivalence is evident. The formalization may therefore be a weaker problem than the source's. Green does not specify the ambient set, so the ℕ reading is defensible.
findings.source_evidence: Green, 100 open problems, Problem 61: "Suppose that A + A contains the first n squares. Is |A| > n^{1−o(1)}? ... considered by Erdős and Newman [112]. For some discussion, see [8, Theorem 1.6]." Alon–Bukh–Sudakov [8] (arXiv:0711.1604): "Though the case when G=(ℤ,+) and A⊂{1,…,n} is the setting in which Erdős and Newman asked their question…"
findings.suggested_fix: Quantify over `A : Finset ℤ` (with the squares cast to ℤ), or document the restriction to ℕ.

findings.description: This 'converse' is not a claim the source makes. The source states only the forward direction (embedding every finite Sidon set in a perfect difference set would give limsup 1), and it records Erdős–Krückeberg's conjecture that 1 is attainable. The consequent is known false (Hall 1947; Alexeev–Mixon 2025, {1,2,4,8,13}), so the theorem is equivalent to `sSup {...} ≠ 1`, as its own docstring notes. As a `research open` target it therefore asks for a proof of (a strengthening of) the negation of the conjecture the source records. The maintainers kept it deliberately (commit 64f61f72), so this is flagged only for review.
findings.source_evidence: erdosproblems.com/329: "In [Er80] he writes that he and Krückeberg conjecture that 1 is possible. The fact that 1 is possible would follow if any finite Sidon set is a subset of a perfect difference set." arXiv:2510.19804: "{1, 2, 4, 8, 13} is a counterexample to this conjecture."
findings.suggested_fix: Remove the variant, or state it transparently as `answer(sorry) ↔ sSup {sidonUpperDensity A | (A : Set ℕ) (_ : IsSidon A)} = 1`.

findings.description: The source asks whether the sum is irrational, which is the sibling `erdos_269.variants.irrational` (∀ P, irrational). This variant instead asks whether the sum is rational for EVERY finite P with |P| ≥ 2. That is neither the source's question nor its negation (∃ P with a rational sum). If the truth is mixed, both variants are false, and settling this one does not settle the source problem. It appears to be a leftover from the older page wording "rational or irrational?".
findings.source_evidence: erdosproblems.com/269 (edited 28 Dec 2025): "Is the sum ∑_{n≥1} 1/[a_1,…,a_n] … irrational?" The Wayback snapshot accessed 2025-09-14 read "…rational or irrational?"
findings.suggested_fix: Drop the variant, or use the negation of the source question: `answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ᵉ (P : Finset ℕ) (_ : ∀ p ∈ P, p.Prime) (_ : P.card ≥ 2), ∃ q : ℚ, (q : ℝ) = series P`.

reformulations.difference: The Lean product is ∏ x ∈ Ioc m (m+n), x = (m+1)⋯(m+n), with n factors starting at m+1 ≥ 2. The source's product is m(m+1)⋯(m+n), with n+1 factors starting at m ≥ 1.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Both statements are 'for all large n, for all admissible starting points'. After reindexing n, they differ only at the starting point 1, i.e. n!. Every prime in (n/2, n] divides n! exactly once, and there are ≫ n/log n such primes, so this case holds for all large n anyway. 'P.card = k' is equivalent to 'at least k such primes'.

reformulations.difference: `IsLychrel10` includes the 0-th iterate, so palindromes are never Lychrel. The usual definition starts iterating at the first reverse-and-add step.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: If a palindrome n > 0 is Lychrel in the usual sense, then 2n = n + rev(n) is Lychrel in the Lean sense. Conversely, Lean-Lychrel implies usual-Lychrel. So 'there are no Lychrel numbers' is the same statement under either definition.

reformulations.difference: Using 0-indexed `Nat.nth Nat.Prime` with u > 0 excludes the prime 2 from every sum of consecutive primes.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Each n has at most one representation starting at 2, since those partial sums are strictly increasing. So f(n) changes by at most 1, and limsup = ⊤ is unaffected.

reformulations.difference: `series` sums over all n ≥ 0, including n = 0, where the lcm over the empty set is 1. So `series P` equals 1 plus the source's sum.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Adding 1 does not change rationality or irrationality.

reformulations.difference: The source says the statement is 'perhaps true with … any k intervals' (∀ k, which is `k_intervals`). This variant uses ∃ k > 2.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Appending the interval [1,1] injectively maps valid (k−1)-tuples to valid k-tuples. So finiteness for k implies finiteness for k−1, and ∃ k > 2 is equivalent to finiteness for k = 3. That is a special case of the source's remark, not a quantifier slip. (The ∀ j scoping over the ∃ n conjunct is harmless for k > 0.)

reformulations.difference: The sup `⨆ m : Fin n, σ 0 m + m - n` is computed in ℕ with truncated subtraction (confirmed via #print).
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Truncation is monotone, so it commutes with the finite maximum. A sequence tends to +∞ iff its truncation does.

review.notes:
FC100OpenSet1.lean has no mathematical statement of its own: it lists 100 declaration names and checks their category counts. All 100 names resolve, none are duplicated, and the counts are 85 open / 15 solved, matching the #eval. I reviewed each referenced declaration against its source; the findings are filed against those declarations.

File-level: the docstring and README call the list "100 open research problems", but 15 are now research solved. This is apparently by design (fixed sample, tracked by the count check), so I did not file it.
